title: Justified by faith (Romans 3:21–28)
hook: Catholics and Lutherans signed a joint declaration on justification in 1999, after centuries of argument
carry: all have sinned, all are loved

segments.voice: Yesterday, the opening of Romans: the gospel as the power of God. Your line was no one shut out. Did you help someone feel welcome? Day five hundred sixty-one.

October thirty-first, 1999. Augsburg, Germany. Representatives of the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation sign a document called the Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification. The date is deliberate: October thirty-first is the anniversary Lutherans keep for the start of the Reformation. The city is deliberate too: Augsburg is where Lutherans set out their beliefs in 1530. For almost five centuries, this one question had divided Western Christians. And at the root of the question lay a few verses of Romans.
screen: `AUGSBURG, OCTOBER 31, 1999.` → `CATHOLICS AND LUTHERANS SIGN.` → `FIVE CENTURIES OVER A FEW VERSES.`

segments.voice: Justification translates a Greek word family built on dikaios, righteous: being made right, or set right, with God. In Romans 3, Paul has just spent two chapters showing that no one, Jew or Gentile, stands right with God by their own record. Then he says, in the Douay-Rheims: "For all have sinned, and do need the glory of God." All. No exceptions, no ranking of who's worse. And in the very next breath: being justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. All have sinned, and all are offered grace as a gift. A few verses later: "For we account a man to be justified by faith, without the works of the law." When Martin Luther translated that verse into German and added a word: allein, alone. Justified by faith alone. That word became a battle line. Lutherans stressed that God declares sinners righteous by grace through faith, not by anything they earn. The Council of Trent, for Catholics, stressed that God's grace truly makes a person righteous within, and that faith works through love. Each side heard the other as denying something essential. The 1999 declaration didn't erase every difference. But both churches stated together that by grace alone, in faith in Christ's saving work, and not because of any merit of ours, we are accepted by God and receive the Holy Spirit, who renews our hearts and calls us to good works. And they said the old condemnations no longer apply to the teaching as each side now explains it. Later, Methodists, Reformed and Anglican churches joined or welcomed it.
screen: `DIKAIOS: SET RIGHT WITH GOD.` · `ALL HAVE SINNED.` · `JUSTIFIED FREELY BY HIS GRACE.` · `LUTHER'S ALLEIN, TRENT'S ANSWER.` · then, large: `A SHARED STATEMENT, 1999.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for Lutheran neighbors, or simply hold them in mind. Settle, and breathe. Maybe there's a Lutheran church you drive past, or a Lutheran friend, coworker or in-law. Picture them. Remember that for centuries, people on both sides were taught to see each other as wrong about the most important thing. And remember Augsburg, where both signed the same words about grace. If you pray, you can ask blessing on that church and those people by name. If not, just wish them well, sincerely. The bell holds the time.
Justification. Being set right with God, freely, by grace: the word that divided Catholics and Lutherans for centuries, and that they spoke together in 1999. Today's word.
Your line: all have sinned, all are loved. Today, when you're tempted to rank someone as worse than you, remember the word all. Day five hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: The Catholic Church teaches that justification is God's free gift received in baptism, which both forgives sin and renews the person within; it joined the Lutheran World Federation in the 1999 Joint Declaration, and many local parishes pray with Lutheran neighbors during the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity.

fork.setup: you're part of a dialogue between two churches that have condemned each other's teaching for centuries. what do you aim for?
options: get the other side to admit it was wrong.
find what both can say together, and name what's still different.
agree to stop talking about it.
fork.reveal: the joint declaration states a shared understanding of grace and faith, says the old condemnations don't apply to the teaching as now explained, and is honest that differences remain.

original.note: Greek: righteousness, justice, being right with God. justification comes from the same family.

trapdoor: what you thought: a technical word theologians argue about.
what it means: how anyone is set right with God: all have sinned, and grace is a free gift. Catholics and Lutherans now say much of this together.

what a scholar hears: dikaioō can mean to declare righteous or to make righteous, and that difference shaped the dispute. Luther's allein in Romans 3:28 has no word in the Greek, though he defended it as the sense.
